I've gathered substantial material from the searches and pages I could fetch. Here are the verse-by-verse notes, with traditions identified where they differ.

---

## Leviticus 10 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — "unauthorized fire before the LORD, contrary to His command"

**Nature of the sin:** Most traditional commentators identify a cluster of transgressions. Ellicott (Anglican) catalogues four: (1) they used their own censers rather than the sacred utensil; (2) both offered together when only one priest should offer incense; (3) they usurped the high priest's role — only the high priest burned incense in a censer (Lev 16:12–13); (4) they offered at an unauthorized time, apart from the morning and evening sacrifice.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/10.htm

Gill (older Baptist) adds that the fire was "common fire" — not taken from the altar of burnt offering as required, but (per the Targum of Jonathan) from under the cooking pots where peace offerings were boiled. He also notes they had no command to offer incense at all; that duty belonged to Aaron alone at this point.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-10.html

**Reformed view (Calvin):** Calvin says the transgression appeared "light" — using strange fire for incense — and their thoughtlessness seemed excusable, for they did not "wantonly or intentionally desire to pollute the sacred things." Yet God's severity teaches that nothing corrupting the purity of religion is small.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-10.html

**R.C. Sproul (Reformed):** Emphasises that "profane" (Latin *profanus*) literally means "outside the temple." The fire had not been purified or consecrated. God killed them to remind Israel of "the sanctity of His presence."
— https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/strange-fire

**David Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic):** The "profane fire" was fire not kindled from the altar of burnt offering — fire not associated with the atoning, redeeming work of sacrifice. He adds the warning that "Satan himself can deceive with fire" (citing Rev 13:13). Guzik also speculates Nadab and Abihu may have dared to go past the veil into the Holy of Holies, citing Lev 16:1–2.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-10/

**Dr. Constable (Evangelical/DTS):** Notes the text does not precisely identify the offense. The "strange fire" was likely an incense offering that somehow violated God's will — perhaps assuming the high priest's role, or offering at the wrong time, or simply wanting to "add to the festivities." The core issue was disobedience regardless of motivation.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-10.html

**Catholic (Haydock):** Notes that whether the fault was neglect (not taking fire from the altar) or thoughtlessness, it was "severely punished, however venial in itself — that all might learn to comply exactly with God's commands." Haydock also records the tradition (from Josephus and the Rabbins) that they were intoxicated, and notes a debate: some infer the offense was mortal and the punishment a prelude to eternal torments; others "piously hope" the sin was only venial, expiated by repentance and violent death, and they were "buried honourably."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/leviticus/10.htm

---

### v. 2 — "fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed them"

**Gill:** Notes they "sinned by fire, and they were punished by fire." The fire was like lightning — it killed them but did not burn their bodies or clothes (evident from vv. 4–5). He compares the case to Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-10.html

**Guzik:** The same fire that displayed God's glory in Lev 9:24 now showed His judgment. "Fire is a figure of searching judgment and purification." He quotes Maclaren: "It was better that two men should die, and the whole nation perish not… It is mercy to trample out the first sparks beside a powder-barrel."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-10/

**Ellicott:** "By fire they sinned, and by fire they died." The divine fire that consumed the sacrifices as acceptance now descended as the avenger of sin — just as the same gospel is "to one a savour of life unto life, and to another a savour of death unto death" (2 Cor 2:16).
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/10.htm

**Ligonier (Reformed):** Stresses that at the very formation of Israel, God laid down fundamental laws of consecration and warned He would "break out" against violators. The modern church has lost the "healthy fear of God" — "God is still a consuming fire" (Deut 4:24).
— https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/strange-fire

---

### v. 3 — "'To those who come near Me I will show My holiness...' But Aaron remained silent."

**Ellicott:** Moses adduces a previously unrecorded divine saying. The sense: God had sanctified Aaron and his sons by holy anointing so they would sanctify Him by strict performance of duties. Having failed, "God sanctified himself in them by the awful punishment." "Aaron held his peace" — he silently submitted to righteous judgment, like the Psalmist: "I was dumb, I opened not my mouth; because thou didst it" (Ps 39:9).
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/10.htm

**Calvin (Reformed):** "Much is this silence of Aaron to be applauded, whereby he confessed that his sons were slain by the just judgment of God." Moses restrains Aaron from excessive grief by reminding him that God's judgment is just. Calvin sees here the principle: the greater the gifts and higher the pre-eminence, the greater the obligation — and the severer the punishment for ingratitude.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-10.html

**Guzik:** Aaron "was able to see this wrong from God's standpoint, not only his own." He quotes Clarke: "How elegantly expressive is this of his parental affection, his deep sense of the presumption of his sons, and his own submission to the justice of God!"
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-10/

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** "Aaron was silent, indicating his submission to the judgment of God, see Ps 39:9; Job 1:22."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/leviticus-10.html

---

### vv. 4–5 — Removal of the bodies by Mishael and Elzaphan

**Gill:** Mishael and Elzaphan were Kohathites of the tribe of Levi, first cousins to Aaron. Being non-priests, they needed a special order to enter the holy place. They carried the bodies "in their coats" (the tunics of the dead), and buried them outside the camp — "probably in their coats in which they had sinned, and in which they died."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-10.html

**Ellicott:** Moses chose these two cousins deliberately, passing over the sons of Izar and Hebron (older uncles), because discontent among Izar's children (soon to erupt in Korah's rebellion, Num 16–17) was already showing. "It was necessary that those who suffered so signally… should be buried by men whose allegiance to God's law was unimpeachable." The tunics — the long white sacerdotal garments — were buried with them; normally cast-off priestly garments became lamp wicks, but no one would reuse garments worn at "so awful a visitation."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/10.htm

**Guzik:** The men chosen were related but not of the priestly line; Moses would not send a consecrated priest to handle dead bodies.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-10/

---

### vv. 6–7 — Prohibition of mourning for Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar

**Ellicott:** "Uncover not your heads" means "let not your heads be dishevelled" — the custom was for mourners to let hair grow long and wild. "Neither rend your clothes" was another standard mourning practice. The prohibition protected against any appearance of reflecting on the justice of God's punishment. The whole house of Israel could mourn — called "your brethren" to show sympathy.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/10.htm

**Guzik:** "This perhaps was the hardest day of Aaron's life. Two of his sons were suddenly killed under the judgment of God, and he could not mourn them. To mourn might have implied — even in the slightest way — that God was wrong." Guzik notes that Aaron might have thought, "I did worse at the golden calf; why did God judge them?" — but Aaron's sin was before his consecration; afterward came greater accountability ("for the anointing oil of the LORD is upon you").
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-10/

**Constable:** "The anointing oil symbolized the Spirit of God who gives life. For this oil to have any contact with death was inappropriate."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-10.html

**Gill:** "They were not to relinquish the service of the sanctuary on the account of the death of these relations." The anointing oil meant they were "under obligation to continue and perform their service without being let or hindered."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-10.html

---

### vv. 8–9 — Prohibition of wine and strong drink for priests on duty

**Connection to Nadab and Abihu:** Virtually all traditions note the proximity to the judgment suggests Nadab and Abihu were intoxicated. Gill: "It is hardly to be accounted for upon any other foot that they should do it." The Targum of Jonathan adds to v. 9: "as did thy sons, who died by the burning of fire." Ellicott notes this opinion "obtained as early at least as the time of Christ."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-10.html
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/10.htm

**Dummelow (Anglican), however, dissents:** "There is… no real ground for this supposition, as Lev 10:8–9 form a separate and disconnected fragment."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/leviticus-10.html

**Guzik (Pentecostal):** The command came immediately after the judgment, strongly suggesting intoxication. He quotes Maclaren: "Nothing has more power to blur the sharpness of moral and religious insight than even a small amount of alcohol. God must be worshipped with clear brain and naturally beating heart."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-10/

**Constable (Evangelical):** Notes the commentators differ — some see a connection to drunkenness, others to rash behavior. He applies it to church leaders: "the common or regular use of intoxicants is incompatible with spiritual service" (cf. 1 Tim 3:3, 8).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-10.html

**`Note on scope`** — Gill, Ellicott, and Jewish sources agree the prohibition applied only when entering the tabernacle for service, not to all times. Ellicott: the injunction "clearly implies that, ordinarily, when not going into the tent of meeting… they were not forbidden to use it if required."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/10.htm

**Uniquely, this is the only time in Leviticus God speaks directly to Aaron** rather than through Moses. Constable: "This shows the importance of what follows and that God still approved of Aaron as the high priest." Ellicott: God honours Aaron with direct speech to comfort him and restore the prestige of the office after the calamity.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-10.html
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/10.htm

---

### vv. 10–11 — The priest's twofold duty: discernment and teaching

**Gill:** Sobriety was required so priests could distinguish holy from common, clean from unclean — "which a drunken man, having his mind and senses disturbed, is not capable of." Then follows the duty to teach Israel "all the statutes." Gill notes the extensive OT witness to the "teaching priest" (Deut 33:10; 2 Chron 17:7; Mal 2:7; Ezra 7:25; Hos 4:6, etc.).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-10.html

**Guzik:** Two responsibilities: (1) discern and explain the difference between holy/unholy, clean/unclean; (2) teach God's word. "This responsibility on the part of the priests is often overlooked. We tend to look at them as only those who offered sacrifices."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-10/

**Ligonier (Reformed):** The passage supports the regulative principle — "our worship must be consonant with divinely revealed principles… To show true reverence to God is to remember that He is the Lawgiver, and those who are truly reverent will do whatever He commands, not adding to it or subtracting from it (Deut 4:2)."
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/reverent-worship

**Constable:** "The essence of the priestly ministry is articulated in Leviticus 10:10–11… Israel, then, was a people separated to Yahweh from among all the nations."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-10.html

---

### vv. 12–15 — Instructions for eating the priestly portions

**Gill:** The grain offering remaining after the handful was burned belonged to the priests, but had to be eaten "beside the altar" (in the court), unleavened, because it was "most holy." The wave breast and heave thigh of the peace offerings could be eaten "in a clean place" by the whole priestly family, including daughters — these were less holy and assigned for household maintenance.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-10.html

**Ellicott:** The grain offering had to be eaten in the court of the tent of meeting. The peace-offering portions could be eaten anywhere within the camp that was ceremonially clean — "for the maintenance of their families."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/10.htm

**Guzik:** Distinguishes the two categories: the grain offering (most holy, eaten beside the altar, priests only) vs. the wave/heave portions (holy, eaten anywhere clean, whole family). The distinction reinforces the holiness gradations in Leviticus.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-10/

---

### vv. 16–18 — Moses' anger over the uneaten sin offering

**The issue:** The goat of the people's sin offering (Lev 9:15) was burned instead of eaten. The rule: if the blood of a sin offering was brought inside the holy place, the carcass was burned outside the camp (Lev 4:1–21); if the blood was applied only to the outer altar, the priests were to eat the meat (Lev 6:25–30). Here the blood had *not* been brought inside, so they should have eaten it.

**Ellicott:** Moses "diligently sought" (made careful inquiry about) the goat. He was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar — probably omitting Aaron's name "to spare the honour of the pontiff." Eating the sin offering was part of the expiatory rite: the priests "by the act of eating visibly show the offerer that God has graciously accepted the expiatory sacrifice." Ellicott notes the debate over "bear the iniquity": some take it as "remove the iniquity" (LXX, Chaldee, Syriac); others (following the Vulgate and Reformers) take it as the priest literally bearing the sin by incorporating the sin-laden victim, prefiguring Christ who is both priest and sacrifice.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/10.htm

**Guzik (Pentecostal):** Adds a pastoral application: "We often find it easy to burn the sin offering, and hard to eat it. Burning hard against sin in a judging manner is easy. To sit down with a brother or sister as a fellow sinner and partake of the sin offering with them means you realize you aren't any better than them."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-10/

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** Moses was angry because the blood had not been brought within the holy place, so the flesh should have been eaten. The sin offering had been burnt instead — "Perhaps they feared God's wrath which had just fallen on their brothers."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/leviticus-10.html

**Constable:** Cites Jacob Milgrom (modern Jewish scholar): by requiring the *hatta't* (sin offering) to be eaten, "Israel gave birth to a new and radical idea: the sanctuary is purged not by any inherent power of the ritual but only by the will of God" — a move away from magical/demonic concepts found in the ancient Near East.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-10.html

---

### vv. 19–20 — Aaron's explanation and Moses' acceptance

**Aaron's defense:** "This very day they presented their sin offering and burnt offering before the LORD. Since these things have happened to me, if I had eaten the sin offering today, would it have been acceptable in the sight of the LORD?"

**Ellicott:** Aaron (though not directly named in v. 16) was fully aware he was included in the censure. He argues that having suffered such calamity, eating the sin offering — which was an act of joyful communion — would have been inappropriate. Moses "was content" ("it was good in his eyes").
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/10.htm

**Guzik:** Aaron did not eat because he mourned. Though forbidden to show the usual signs of mourning, "it was appropriate that he fast on the day of his sons' death." Moses accepted this. Guzik notes the phrase "he was content" is literally "and it was good in his eyes" — the same verb used in v. 19 for what is "acceptable in the sight of the LORD."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-10/

**Constable:** Offers an alternative interpretation: "Perhaps the holiness of God so impressed Aaron that he felt unworthy to eat what he had offered as a sin offering. He probably concluded that mourners should not take part in sacrificial meals (cf. Deut 26:14)." This motivation — reverence rather than mere grief — is "preferable" because mere grief probably would not have satisfied Moses. "God is more gracious with those who fear Him and make mistakes than He is with those who do not fear Him as they should."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-10.html

**Bridgeway Commentary:** "Aaron replied that because of the terrible happenings that day, his two younger sons thought it would be more acceptable to God for them to burn their portion in sorrow than to eat it in joy. Their action was wrong but it came from good motives. Moses, with great sympathy and understanding, saw this and said no more."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/leviticus-10.html

---

## Where Traditions Notably Differ

### Regulative Principle of Worship (Reformed vs. others)

The Reformed tradition (Calvin, Sproul, Ligonier) draws a distinctive conclusion from Lev 10: worship must be strictly according to God's commands — nothing may be added. Ligonier states: "our worship must be consonant with divinely revealed principles… those who are truly reverent will do whatever He commands, not adding to it or subtracting from it (Deut 4:2)." Sproul ties this to "strange fire" as anything offered that God has not commanded. This is the classic Reformed "regulative principle."
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/reverent-worship
— https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/strange-fire

Other evangelical traditions (Guzik/Enduring Word, Constable) emphasise obedience and reverence but do not frame the passage in terms of the regulative principle as a worship rubric. They focus more on heart attitude and the danger of self-willed, fleshly worship.

### Intoxication of Nadab and Abihu

The majority of older commentators (Gill, Ellicott, Clarke, the Targum of Jonathan, Haydock) hold that Nadab and Abihu were drunk. Dummelow's Commentary (Anglican) is a notable dissenter: "there is… no real ground for this supposition, as Lev 10:8–9 form a separate and disconnected fragment." Constable hedges, noting scholars differ — some see intoxication, others merely rash behavior.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/leviticus-10.html

### Catholic view — venial or mortal sin?

Haydock records an internal Catholic debate: whether Nadab and Abihu's sin was mortal (their punishment prefiguring eternal torments) or venial (expiated by repentance and death, hence they were "buried honourably"). Haydock leans toward the softer reading: "others piously hope that their sin was only venial."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/leviticus/10.htm

### "Bear the iniquity" (v. 17)

Ellicott notes a translation divide: the ancient versions (LXX, Chaldee, Syriac) render "remove the iniquity"; the Vulgate and the Reformers (Luther, English) render "bear the iniquity." The latter reading supports a typological interpretation where the priest, by eating the sin-laden victim, prefigures Christ bearing sin as both priest and sacrifice.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/10.htm

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (via Milgrom, cited by Constable)

Jacob Milgrom argues that the requirement for priests to *eat* the sin offering (rather than destroy it, as was customary in ancient Near Eastern purification rites) was a "giant step towards eviscerating the magical and demonic elements from Israelite ritual." In surrounding cultures, ritual detergents were destroyed lest their potent remains be used for black magic. By requiring consumption, Israel declared that "the sanctuary is purged not by any inherent power of the ritual but only by the will of God."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-10.html
